newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 4.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- AIRPORT SLOT TRADE MAY OPEN UP

The European Commission is expected to rule before the end of this year on possible changes to the buying and selling of airport take-off and landing slots. If, as expected, the Commission recommends a legalised system to replace the current grey market, it could boost the chances of the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines.
-- C&A CALLS FOR FORUM TO IMPROVE WORKING CONDITIONS

High street clothing retailer C&A, which was named in a newspaper report on Thursday linking it to suppliers who pay their staff less than 1.50 stg an hour, has called for a national forum to be set up to improve working conditions in the clothing industry. The body would encompass retailers, manufacturers, local authorities and central government.
-- BRITISH GAS REJECTS PRICE PROPOSALS

British Gas has called on the Monopolies and Mergers Commission to settle its increasingly acrimonious dispute with industry regulator Ofgas over prices for its TransCo pipeline operation. Ofgas has proposed price cuts for TransCo which would cut transportation charges to the country's 19 million gas customers by 28 stg a year, equivalent to a 400 million stg a year net reduction in revenue for TransCo.
-- P&O AND STENA IN FERRY LINK-UP TO FIGHT EUROTUNNEL

The two largest operators of cross-Channel ferry services between Britain and the continent, P&O and Stena Lines, have announced plans to merge their operations to fight the challenge of the Channel tunnel. The deal will entail reduced sailings, combined timetables, and joint marketing campaigns. The move is expected to receive sharp scrutiny from competition regulators in both the UK and the European Union.
-- MERCK TO SELL AIDS DRUG AT ONE PRICE FOR EUROPE

US pharmaceuticals company Merck is to market its new Aids drug, Crixivan, at the same price across all the countries of the European Union. The move is unprecedented in the healthcare industry in recent decades, and is intended to prevent the trade in purchasing drugs at lower prices in southern-Europe and reselling at the higher prices usually commanded in northern markets. The drug will be one of the first products to be priced in Ecus.
-- PRICE CURBS SHOCK NATIONAL GRID

National Grid Group, operators of the electricity transmission system in England and Wales, has refused to comment publicly on proposals from the industry regulator Professor Stephen Littlechild for cuts of 20 percent in the group's charges to consumers. Privately, senior executives at the group are said to be shocked by the scale of the proposed cuts, but they are not expected to seek a referral of the matter to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission, a move which could impinge on the group's ability to sell its telecommunications subsidiary Energis.
-- UTILITIES WARNED ON WINDFALL TAX

The electricity industry regulator Professor Stephen Littlechild has warned that electricity companies will not be able to raise their prices to pay for Labours proposed windfall tax on the privatised utilities. Littlechild ruled that the proposed levy will be intended as a tax on shareholders, and companies should therefore look at reducing dividends instead of raising prices for consumers.
-- OLIVETTI IN 1,200 bln lira ASSET SELL-OFF

Troubled Italian information technology and telecommunications group Olivetti is to sell off its personal computer division as part of a 1,200 billion lira (509 million stg) programme of asset disposals. The group is also expected to sell-off a stake in its mobile telecoms subsidiary Omnitel. The sale of the PC division, which recorded first-half losses of 15.8 billion earlier this year, has been identified as the 'number one priority sale'.
-- VAI SAYS KVAERNER PAPERS WERE TAKEN

Austrian engineering group VAI, which is embroiled in an espionage row with Scandinavian rival Kvaerner, has revealed that some of its employees removed confidential documents from Davy International, a UK subsidiary of Kvaerner. Kvaerner has launched a multi-million dollar compensation claim against KAI over the incident, which involved papers relating contracts where VAI and Davy were competing.
-- CREDIT LYONNAIS 'NEEDS FFr9 bln'

The chairman of French state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais, which last week secured a FFr3.9 billion emergency aid package, has said the troubled bank needs a recapitalisation of at least FFr9 billion (1.1 bln stg) from the French government to make it fit for privatisation by the start of 1998. The bank reported on Thursday first-half profits of FFr67 million, results which, according to chairman Jean Peyrelevade, indicated the bank had 'crossed the Alps and rejoined the pack'.
